main.summary: The Three Character Classic is written in rhyming lines of three characters, in pairs. It begins with human nature and education, then moves through everyday knowledge, numbered lists, the Confucian classics and the rise and fall of the dynasties, and ends with stories of famous scholars to urge children to set their aims early and study.
main.translation:
At the beginning people are by nature good; by nature they are close to one another, by habit they grow far apart.
If they are not taught, their nature changes; the way of teaching is valued for its single-minded focus.
Long ago Mencius's mother chose a neighbourhood with care; when her son would not study, she cut the threads on her loom.
Dou of Yanshan had the right way of teaching: he taught five sons, and all of them made their names.
To feed a child without teaching him is the father's fault;
to teach without strictness is the teacher's laziness.
For a child not to study is not as it should be;
if he does not study when young, what will he be when old? Jade that is not cut and polished does not become a vessel;
a person who does not study does not know what is right.
As a son, in your young days, stay close to teachers and friends and practise courtesy and ritual.
Huang Xiang at nine could warm his father's bed; serving one's parents with filial piety is what you should hold to.
Kong Rong at four could give up the big pears; respect for elders is what you should know first.
Begin with filial piety and brotherly respect, then seeing and hearing; learn numbers and learn names.
One to ten, ten to a hundred, a hundred to a thousand, a thousand to ten thousand.
The three powers are Heaven, earth and people;
the three lights are the sun, moon and stars;
the three bonds are rightness between ruler and minister, affection between father and son, and accord between husband and wife.
We speak of spring and summer, we speak of autumn and winter: these are the four seasons, turning without end.
We speak of south and north, we speak of west and east: these are the four directions, which answer to the centre.
We speak of water and fire, wood, metal and earth: these are the five phases, rooted in number.
We speak of humaneness and rightness, ritual, wisdom and good faith: these are the five constants, which must not be confused.
Rice, sorghum, water-oat, wheat, broomcorn millet and millet: these are the six grains that people eat.
Horse, ox, sheep, chicken, dog and pig: these are the six domestic animals that people keep.
We speak of joy and anger, we speak of grief and delight, and of love, hate and desire: these are the seven feelings.
Gourd, clay, hide, wood, stone and metal, with silk and bamboo: these are the eight kinds of sound.
Great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father and oneself; oneself, son and grandson; from son and grandson on to great-grandson and great-great-grandson: these are the nine generations, the order of human ties.
Between father and son, affection; between husband and wife, accord; an elder brother is friendly, a younger brother respectful; the elder is kind, the younger obedient; the ruler is courteous, the minister loyal: these are the ten duties that all people share.
In teaching the young, one must pay close attention:
explain the meaning of words in detail, and make clear where the sentences break.
A learner must begin at the beginning: from the Classic of Filial Piety to the Four Books. The Analects has twenty chapters, in which the disciples recorded good sayings.
Mencius has seven books and stops there; it speaks of the Way and virtue, and explains humaneness and rightness.
The Doctrine of the Mean was written by Kong Ji: the 'middle' does not lean, the 'constant' does not change.
The Great Learning was written by Master Zeng: from cultivating the self and ordering the family through to governing the state and bringing peace.
When the Classic of Filial Piety is mastered and the Four Books are known well, then the Six Classics may begin to be read.
The Songs, Documents, Changes, Rites and Spring and Autumn are called the Six Classics and should be studied closely. There are the Lianshan, the Guizang and the Zhou Changes: the three Changes are set out in detail.
There are the Canons and Counsels, the Instructions and Announcements, the Oaths and Charges: these are the depths of the Documents.
Our Duke of Ji wrote the Rites of Zhou, setting out the six offices and preserving the form of government.
The Elder and Younger Dai annotated the Record of Rites, passing on the sage's words, and rites and music were complete.
The Airs of the states, the Odes and the Hymns are called the four kinds of poems, and should be chanted.
When the Songs had died away, the Spring and Autumn was written, placing praise and blame in its wording and separating good from evil.
The three commentaries are the Gongyang, the Zuo and the Guliang.
When the Classics are clear, then read the masters: take their essentials and note their facts.
The five masters are Xun and Yang,
Wenzhongzi, and Lao and Zhuang.
When the Classics and the masters are mastered, read the histories: study the lines of descent and know the beginnings and ends.
From Fuxi and Shennong to the Yellow Emperor, called the Three Sovereigns, they lived in the earliest age.
Tang and Yu are called the two Emperors; they bowed and yielded the throne to each other, and are praised for a flourishing rule.
Xia had Yu, Shang had Tang, and Zhou had Wen and Wu: these are called the three Kings.
Xia handed power on to a son and made the realm one family's; after four hundred years the Xia altars were moved.
Tang attacked Xia and named the dynasty Shang; after six hundred years it ended with Zhou the tyrant.
King Wu of Zhou was the first to put the tyrant to death; his dynasty lasted eight hundred years, the longest of all.
The Zhou cart-tracks turned east and the royal bond fell; shields and spears were brandished, and travelling persuaders were prized.
The Spring and Autumn period began and the Warring States ended; five hegemons were strong, and seven powers arose.
The house of Ying in Qin began to swallow up the other states; it passed down two generations, and then Chu and Han contended.
Gaozu rose and built the Han; when it came to Emperor Ping, Wang Mang usurped the throne.
Guangwu rose and made the Eastern Han; four hundred years in all, ending with Emperor Xian.
Wei, Shu and Wu fought over the tripod of Han and were called the Three Kingdoms, down to the two Jin.
Song, Qi, Liang and Chen followed one another as the Southern Dynasties, with their capital at Jinling.
In the north there was the Yuan Wei, which split into east and west, then the Yuwen Zhou and the Gao Qi.
When it came to the Sui, the land was made one, but the throne was not passed on again and the line was lost.
Gaozu of Tang raised a righteous army, ended the Sui disorder and founded the state.
Twenty reigns and three hundred years; Liang destroyed it and the dynasty changed.
Liang, Tang, Jin, Han and Zhou are called the Five Dynasties, and each had its reasons.
The blazing Song rose, receiving the abdication of Zhou; eighteen reigns, and north and south were mixed together.
The seventeen histories are all here; they record order and disorder, and show how states rise and fall.
Whoever reads history should study the true records and link past and present as if seeing it with his own eyes.
Recite it with your mouth and ponder it with your heart; in the morning on this, in the evening on this.
Long ago Zhongni took Xiang Tuo as his teacher; the ancient sages and worthies still loved to study.
Zhao, the Central Secretary, read the Lu Analects; he was already in office, yet he studied and worked hard.
One opened rolls of cattail leaf, another cut bamboo slips; they had no books, yet knew to strive.
One hung his head from the beam, another pricked his thigh with an awl; no one taught them, but they worked hard themselves.
One kept fireflies in a bag, another read by the glow of snow; their homes were poor, but their study did not stop.
One carried firewood, another hung a book on a horn; their bodies were tired, yet they studied on.
Su Laoquan began to study hard at twenty-seven, reading books; though already old, he still regretted his lateness. You who are young should find a teacher early.
Liang Hao, at eighty-two, answered in the great court and came first among all the scholars; he ripened late, and everyone called it wonderful. You who are young should set your aim.
Ying at eight could recite poems;
Bi at seven could write a verse on chess;
they were quick and clever and people marvelled; you who learn young should follow them.
Cai Wenji could tell the notes of a zither;
Xie Daoyun could chant verse;
they were girls, yet clever; you who are boys should achieve early.
A gifted child was recommended and made a proofreader; though young, he already held office.
You who learn young, strive and you will reach it; those who achieve things are like this.
The dog guards the night and the cock keeps the dawn; if one does not learn, how can one be called a person? The silkworm spins silk and the bee makes honey; a person who does not learn is worse than a creature.
Learn when young and act when grown; above, serve your ruler, and below, benefit the people;
make your name known and bring honour to your parents; add glory to what came before and leave it for those after.
Others leave their sons baskets full of gold; I teach my son one classic only;
diligence has its reward, and play has no gain. Take warning, and make an effort.

keyLines.line: 人之初，性本善，性相近，習相遠；苟不教，性乃遷，教之道，貴以專。
keyLines.en: At the beginning, people are by nature good; by nature they are close, by habit they grow far apart. If they are not taught, their nature changes; the way of teaching is valued for its single focus.
keyLines.note: The opening states the aim: people are good by nature and much alike, and it is the habits they pick up afterwards that set them apart. Without teaching, their nature changes, and the way to teach is to keep to one thing with full attention.

keyLines.line: 昔孟母，擇鄰處，子不學，斷機杼；竇燕山，有義方，教五子，名俱揚。
keyLines.en: Long ago Mencius's mother chose her neighbours with care; when her son would not study, she cut the threads on her loom. Dou of Yanshan had a right way to teach his five sons, and all of them made their names.
keyLines.note: Two stories show how much teaching matters. Mencius's mother moved house three times to find good neighbours and cut her weaving to make her point about study. Dou Yujun, in the Five Dynasties period (907-960), raised five sons who all became famous.

keyLines.line: 養不教，父之過；教不嚴，師之惰。子不學，非所宜；幼不學，老何為？玉不琢，不成器；人不學，不知理；
keyLines.en: To feed without teaching is the father's fault; to teach without strictness is the teacher's laziness. For a child not to study is not right; if one does not study when young, what will one do when old? Jade that is not cut and polished does not become a vessel; a person who does not study does not know principle.
keyLines.note: Who is responsible: a father who only feeds his children is at fault, and a teacher who is lax is idle. It is wrong for a child not to learn, and a child who does not learn will have nothing to offer in old age. Uncut jade cannot become a vessel, and an unlearned person does not understand what is right.

keyLines.line: 為人子，方少時，親師友，習禮儀。香九齡，能溫席，孝於親，所當執；融四歲，能讓梨，悌於長，宜先知。
keyLines.en: As a son, in your young days, stay close to teachers and friends and practise courtesy and ritual. Huang Xiang at nine could warm his father's mat; filial duty to parents is what you should hold to. Kong Rong at four could give up the pears; respect for elders is what you should know first.
keyLines.note: A young person should keep company with teachers and friends and learn proper manners. The examples are Huang Xiang, who at nine warmed his father's bed before he went to sleep, and Kong Rong, who at four let his elder brothers have the larger pears. Respecting parents and elder brothers is the first thing to know.

keyLines.line: 首孝弟，次見聞，知某數，識某名。一而十，十而百，百而千，千而萬。三才者，天地人；三光者，日月星；三綱者，君臣義，父子親，夫婦順。
keyLines.en: First filial piety and brotherly respect, then seeing and hearing; know numbers and learn names. One to ten, ten to a hundred, a hundred to a thousand, a thousand to ten thousand. The three powers: Heaven, earth and people; the three lights: sun, moon and stars. The three bonds: between ruler and minister, rightness; between father and son, affection; between husband and wife, accord.
keyLines.note: The order of learning: filial piety and respect for brothers first, then wider experience, numbers and names. Counting rises from one to ten thousand. The three powers are Heaven, earth and humankind; the three lights are the sun, moon and stars; the three bonds are the ethics of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife.

keyLines.line: 曰春夏，曰秋冬，此四時，運不窮；曰南北，曰西東，此四方，應乎中。曰水火，木金土，此五行，本乎數；曰仁義，禮智信，此五常，不容紊。
keyLines.en: Spring and summer, autumn and winter: these are the four seasons, turning without end. South and north, west and east: these are the four directions, set by the centre. Water and fire, wood, metal and earth: these are the five phases, rooted in number. Humaneness, rightness, ritual, wisdom and good faith: these are the five constants, which must not be confused.
keyLines.note: The first set of lists. The four seasons turn without end and the four directions are taken from the centre. The five phases - water, fire, wood, metal and earth - are based on number, and the five constants - humaneness, rightness, ritual propriety, wisdom and good faith - are not to be mixed up.

keyLines.line: 稻粱菰，麥黍稷，此六穀，人所食；馬牛羊，雞犬豕，此六畜，人所飼。曰喜怒，曰哀樂，愛惡欲，乃七情；匏土革，木石金，與絲竹，乃八音。
keyLines.en: Rice, sorghum, water-oat, wheat, broomcorn millet and millet: these are the six grains that people eat. Horse, ox, sheep, chicken, dog and pig: these are the six domestic animals that people keep. Joy and anger, grief and delight, love, hate and desire: these are the seven feelings. Gourd, clay, hide, wood, stone, metal, with silk and bamboo: these are the eight kinds of sound.
keyLines.note: The second set of lists. There are six grains for eating and six domestic animals for rearing. The seven feelings are joy, anger, grief, delight, love, hate and desire. The eight sounds classify instruments by the material: gourd, clay, hide, wood, stone, metal, silk and bamboo.

keyLines.line: 高曾祖，父而身，身而子，子而孫，自子孫，至曾玄，乃九族，人之倫。父子恩，夫婦從，兄則友，弟則恭，長則惠，幼則順，君則敬，臣則忠，此十義，人所同。
keyLines.en: Great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father and oneself; oneself, son, grandson; from son and grandson on to great-grandson and great-great-grandson: these are the nine generations, the order of human ties. Between father and son, affection; between husband and wife, compliance; an elder brother is friendly, a younger one respectful; the elder is kind, the younger obedient; the ruler is courteous, the minister loyal: these are the ten duties that all people share.
keyLines.note: On family ties. The nine generations run from one's great-great-grandfather to one's own great-great-grandson, with oneself in the middle, and they make up the 'nine kinship groups'. The ten duties are those of father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brothers, older and younger people, ruler and minister, each side with a part to play.

keyLines.line: 凡訓蒙，須講究；詳訓詁，明句讀。為學者，必有初，由孝經，至四書：論語者，二十篇，群弟子，記善言；孟子者，七篇止，講道德，說仁義；作中庸，乃孔伋，中不偏，庸不易；作大學，乃曾子，自脩齊，至平治。孝經通，四書熟，如六經，始可讀。
keyLines.en: In teaching the young, one must pay attention: explain the meaning of words in detail and make clear where the sentences break. A learner must begin at the start: from the Classic of Filial Piety to the Four Books. The Analects has twenty chapters, in which the disciples recorded good sayings. Mencius has seven books and stops there; it speaks of virtue and of humaneness and rightness. The Doctrine of the Mean was written by Kong Ji; the 'middle' does not lean, the 'constant' does not change. The Great Learning was written by Master Zeng, from self-cultivation and ordering the family through to governing and bringing peace. When the Classic of Filial Piety is mastered and the Four Books are known well, then the Six Classics may begin to be read.
keyLines.note: The order of reading. Begin with the Classic of Filial Piety and the Four Books. The Analects has twenty chapters recording Confucius's sayings by his followers. The Mencius has seven books on virtue, humaneness and rightness. The Doctrine of the Mean is attributed to Kong Ji (Zisi), and the Great Learning to Master Zeng, running from cultivating oneself and ordering the family to governing the state and bringing peace. After the Four Books are known well, the Six Classics may be read.

keyLines.line: 詩書易，禮春秋，號六經，當講求：有連山，有歸藏，有周易，三易詳；有典謨，有訓誥，有誓命，書之奧；我姬公，作周禮，著六典，存治體；大小戴，註禮記，述聖言，禮樂備；曰國風，曰雅頌，號四詩，當詠諷；詩既亡，春秋作，寓褒貶，別善惡。
keyLines.en: The Songs, Documents, Changes, Rites and Spring and Autumn are called the Six Classics, and are to be studied closely. There are the Lianshan, the Guizang and the Zhou Changes: the three Changes are set out in detail. There are the Canons and Counsels, the Instructions and Announcements, and the Oaths and Charges: these are the depth of the Documents. Our Duke of Ji wrote the Rites of Zhou, setting out the six offices and preserving the form of government. The Elder and Younger Dai annotated the Record of Rites, passing on the sage's words, and rites and music were complete. The Airs of the states, the Odes and the Hymns are called the four kinds of poems, and should be chanted. When the Songs had died away, the Spring and Autumn was written, hiding praise and blame in its account and separating good from evil.
keyLines.note: An introduction to the Six Classics. The Changes exist in three versions: the Lianshan, the Guizang and the Zhou Changes. The Documents contains several kinds of text: canons, counsels, instructions, announcements, oaths and charges. The Duke of Zhou is credited with the Rites of Zhou and its six offices. Dai De and Dai Sheng compiled the Record of Rites. The Book of Songs divides into Customs of the States, Lesser and Greater Elegantiae, and Hymns. After the Songs ceased to be made, Confucius produced the Spring and Autumn Annals, in which praise and blame lie within the narrative.

keyLines.line: 三傳者，有公羊，有左氏，有穀梁；經既明，方讀子，撮其要，記其事。五子者，有荀楊。文中子，及老莊。經子通，讀諸史，考世系，知終始。
keyLines.en: The three commentaries are the Gongyang, the Zuo and the Guliang. When the Classics are clear, then read the masters: take their essentials and note their facts. The five masters are Xun and Yang, Wenzhongzi, and Lao and Zhuang. When the Classics and the masters are mastered, read the histories: study the lines of descent and know the beginnings and ends.
keyLines.note: The commentaries that explain the Spring and Autumn Annals are the Gongyang, the Zuo and the Guliang. Once the Classics are clear, read the philosophers: the five are Xunzi, Yang Xiong, Wang Tong (Wenzhongzi), Laozi and Zhuangzi. After both Classics and philosophers are known, read the histories, trace the lines of succession and see how dynasties begin and end.

keyLines.line: 自羲農，至黃帝，號三皇，居上世；唐有虞，號二帝，相揖遜，稱盛治。夏有禹，商有湯，周文武，稱三王；夏傳子，家天下，四百載，遷夏社；湯伐夏，國號商，六百載，至紂亡；周武王，始誅紂，八百載，最長久。
keyLines.en: From Fuxi and Shennong to the Yellow Emperor, called the Three Sovereigns, they lived in the earliest age. Tang and Yu are called the two Emperors; they bowed and yielded the throne to each other, and are praised for a flourishing rule. Xia had Yu, Shang had Tang, and Zhou had Wen and Wu: these are called the three Kings. Xia handed power on to a son and made the realm one family's; after four hundred years the Xia altars were moved. Tang attacked Xia and the dynasty was named Shang; after six hundred years it ended with Zhou the tyrant. King Wu of Zhou first put the tyrant to death; eight hundred years, the longest of all.
keyLines.note: Summary of history, part one. Fuxi, Shennong and the Yellow Emperor are the Three Sovereigns of the earliest age. Yao and Shun, the two Emperors, passed the throne to each other. The three Kings are Yu of Xia, Tang of Shang, and Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou. Xia handed the throne to a son, making the realm a family possession, and lasted about 400 years. Shang lasted about 600 years until the tyrant Zhou. The Zhou dynasty (c. 1046-256 BC) lasted about 800 years, the longest of all.

keyLines.line: 周轍東，王綱墜，逞干戈，尚游說。始春秋，終戰國，五霸強，七雄出；嬴秦氏，始兼并，傳二世，楚漢爭。高祖興，漢業建，至孝平，王莽篡。光武興，為東漢，四百年，終於獻；魏蜀吳，爭漢鼎，號三國，迄兩晉。
keyLines.en: Zhou's cart-tracks moved east, and the royal bond fell; shields and spears were brandished, and persuaders were prized. The Spring and Autumn began, the Warring States ended; five hegemons were strong, seven powers arose. The house of Ying in Qin began to merge the states; it passed down two generations, and then Chu and Han contended. Gaozu rose and built the Han; at Emperor Xiao Ping's time Wang Mang usurped it. Guangwu rose and made the Eastern Han; four hundred years, ending with Xian. Wei, Shu and Wu fought over the tripod of Han, called the Three Kingdoms, down to the two Jin.
keyLines.note: Summary of history, part two. After the Zhou court moved east, royal authority collapsed, and lords fought and wandering advisers were in demand. The Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods had five hegemons and seven strong states. The First Emperor of Qin united the country, but his dynasty lasted only two reigns before Chu and Han fought for power. Gaozu founded the Western Han, which was taken over by Wang Mang in the time of Emperor Ping. Emperor Guangwu restored the Han as the Eastern Han, which ended with Emperor Xian. Then came the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu, followed by the Western and Eastern Jin.

keyLines.line: 宋齊繼，梁陳承，為南朝，都金陵；北元魏，分東西，宇文周，與高齊；迨至隋，一土宇，不再傳，失統緒。唐高祖，起義師，除隋亂，創國基。二十傳，三百載，梁滅之，國乃改；梁唐晉，及漢周，稱五代，皆有由。炎宋興，受周禪，十八傳，南北混。
keyLines.en: Song, Qi, Liang and Chen followed one another as the Southern Dynasties, with their capital at Jinling. In the north, the Yuan Wei split into east and west; there were the Yuwen Zhou and the Gao Qi. When it came to Sui, the land was made one, but the throne was not passed on again and the line was lost. Gaozu of Tang raised a righteous army, ended the Sui disorder and founded the state. Twenty reigns, three hundred years; Liang destroyed it and the dynasty changed. Liang, Tang, Jin, Han and Zhou are called the Five Dynasties, and each had its reasons. The blazing Song rose, receiving the abdication of Zhou; eighteen reigns, north and south joined.
keyLines.note: Summary of history, part three. The southern courts of Song, Qi, Liang and Chen all had their capital at Jinling (Nanjing). In the north the Yuan (Tuoba) Wei split into east and west, followed by the Northern Zhou and the Northern Qi. Sui reunited the land but did not last. Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty (618-907) rose in arms, put down the Sui disorder and founded a new state; it passed through twenty emperors in about three hundred years, and was ended by the later Liang. Five short dynasties followed. The Song, which received the throne from the Later Zhou, had eighteen emperors and linked northern and southern halves.

keyLines.line: 十七史，全在茲，載治亂，知興衰；讀史者，考實錄，通古今，若親目。口而誦，心而惟，朝於斯，夕於斯。
keyLines.en: The seventeen histories are all here; they record order and disorder, and show how states rise and fall. Whoever reads history should study the true records and link past and present as if seeing it with his own eyes. Recite it with your mouth and ponder it with your heart; in the morning on this, in the evening on this.
keyLines.note: The close of the history section. The seventeen standard histories record order and disorder, and show why states rose and fell. Readers should check the true records and link old and new, as if they had seen events themselves. Recite with the mouth and think with the heart, morning and evening.

keyLines.line: 昔仲尼，師項橐，古聖賢，尚勤學；趙中令，讀魯論，彼既仕，學且勤；披蒲編，削竹簡，彼無書，且知勉；頭懸梁，錐刺股，彼不教，自勤苦；如囊螢，如映雪，家雖貧，學不輟；如負薪，如掛角，身雖勞，猶苦學。
keyLines.en: Long ago Zhongni took Xiang Tuo as his teacher; the ancient sages still loved to study. Zhao, the Central Secretary, read the Lu Analects; he was already in office, yet he studied and worked hard. One opened rolls of cattail leaf, another cut bamboo slips; they had no books, yet knew to strive. One hung his head from the beam, another pricked his thigh with an awl; no one taught them, but they worked hard themselves. One kept fireflies in a bag, another read by the glow of snow; their homes were poor, but their study did not stop. One carried firewood, another hung a book on a horn; their bodies were tired, yet they studied on.
keyLines.note: Stories of study, part one. Confucius learned from the child Xiang Tuo. Zhao Pu, chancellor to the first Song emperor, kept reading the Analects while in office. Lu Wenshu wrote on cattail leaves and Gongsun Hong on strips of bamboo because they had no paper. Sun Jing tied his hair to the beam and Su Qin jabbed himself with an awl to stay awake. Che Yin read by the light of fireflies in a bag and Sun Kang by the glow of snow. Zhu Maichen read while carrying firewood and Li Mi hung a book on the horn of an ox.

keyLines.line: 蘇老泉，二十七，始發憤，讀書籍，彼既老，猶悔遲，爾小生，宜早師。若梁灝，八十二，對大廷，魁多士，彼晚成，眾稱異，爾小生，宜立志。
keyLines.en: Su Laoquan began to study hard at twenty-seven; though already old, he still regretted his lateness. You who are young should find a teacher early. Liang Hao, at eighty-two, answered in the great court and came first among all the scholars; he ripened late, and everyone called it wonderful. You who are young should set your aim.
keyLines.note: Stories of study, part two. Su Xun, known by his pen name Laoquan, only began to study seriously at twenty-seven, and he still regretted starting too late. According to the story, Liang Hao took first place in the palace examination at the age of eighty-two. The children are told to set their goals early.

keyLines.line: 瑩八歲，能詠詩；泌七歲，能賦棋；彼穎悟，人稱奇，爾幼學，當效之。蔡文姬，能辨琴；謝道韞，能詠吟；彼女子，且聰明，爾男子，當少成。舉神童，作正字，彼雖幼，身已仕；爾幼學，勉而致，有為者，亦若是。
keyLines.en: Ying at eight could recite poems; Bi at seven could write a verse on chess; they were quick and clever and people marvelled; you who learn young should follow them. Cai Wenji could tell the notes of a zither; Xie Daoyun could chant verse; they were girls, yet clever; you who are boys should achieve early. A gifted child was recommended and made a proofreader; though young, he already held office. You who learn young, strive and you will reach it; those who achieve things are like this.
keyLines.note: Stories of study, part three. Zu Ying could write poems at eight and Li Bi at seven could compose a verse about chess; Cai Wenji could tell which zither string had broken, and Xie Daoyun was known for her poem about willow-catkins in snow. All were quick-minded. A child prodigy could also be given office as a proofreader at court. Pupils are urged to work hard, because those who achieve are made the same way.

keyLines.line: 犬守夜，雞司晨，苟不學，曷為人？蠶吐絲，蜂釀蜜，人不學，不如物。幼而學，壯而行，上致君，下澤民；揚名聲，顯父母，光於前，垂於後。人遺子，金滿籯，我教子，惟一經；勤有功，戲無益，戒之哉，宜勉力。
keyLines.en: The dog guards the night and the cock keeps the dawn; if one does not learn, how can one be called a person? The silkworm spins silk and the bee makes honey; a person who does not learn is worse than a creature. Learn when young and act when grown; above, serve your ruler, and below, benefit the people. Make your name known and bring honour to your parents; add glory to what came before and leave it for those after. Others leave their sons baskets full of gold; I teach my son one classic only. Diligence has its reward; play has no gain. Take warning, and make an effort.
keyLines.note: The conclusion. The dog guards the house at night and the cock marks the dawn; the silkworm spins silk and the bee makes honey. A person who will not learn is worth less than any of them. Study when young, act when grown, serve the ruler above and bless the people below, make a name, honour one's parents, and bring glory to ancestors and descendants. Others leave sons chests of gold, but the writer only teaches one classic. Hard work pays; play does not. Take it to heart and strive.

glossary.en: xing xiang jin, xi xiang yuan - 'close by nature, far apart by habit'
glossary.note: From the Analects (Yang Huo chapter): people are much alike in nature, and the gaps between them grow through the habits they form.

glossary.en: zhu - the shuttle of a loom
glossary.note: Pronounced zhu; to 'cut the loom threads' means Mencius's mother cut her half-woven cloth to teach her son.
The proper method of teaching one's children.
The guiding ties of ruler and minister, father and son, and husband and wife.
Water, fire, wood, metal and earth, which the ancients thought were the five basic elements of all things.
The old classification of instruments by material: metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, clay, hide and wood.
Relatives over nine generations: great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father, oneself, son, grandson, great-grandson and great-great-grandson.

glossary.en: xun gu, ju dou - glossing and punctuation
glossary.note: Xungu is explaining the meaning of words in old books; judou is marking where the sentences break.

main.background: The Three Character Classic is traditionally ascribed to Wang Yinglin of the Song dynasty (960-1279), and later hands added to it. The version here is the traditional old text, with the history ending in the Song. It has three characters to a line, and covers human relations, general knowledge, the classics and histories, and the value of study. It is one of the three great traditional primers for children, known together as the 'San Bai Qian' (the Three Character Classic, the Hundred Family Surnames and the Thousand Character Classic). This text follows the Wikisource edition and differs in a few places from modern editions.
